input.evidence_text: Site for new Bolton community bike hub 'stormed' by vandals - BBC News Image source, Believe Achieve CIC Image caption, The project was given planning permission in July By Jade Taylorson North West Published 1 hour ago A site where a new community bike hub is being built to help reduce antisocial behaviour has been vandalised. Police are investigating after the Believe Achieve CIC project in Stoneclough, Bolton, was targeted on Monday night. The bike hub was being built after reports of young people in the area using illegal motorised bikes - and the group aims to give youngsters access to bicycles while teaching road safety and maintenance skills. Tunde Olasupo, project founder, says the site was "stormed" by people who vandalised a surrounding fence and forcibly opened a container that will house the hub. They added there had been opposition to the project, with concerns about further antisocial behaviour. There were also concerns about its location and environmental impact, Olasupo said. 'Upset' "Of course, I'm upset, and when you see something that you've worked hard for deliberately damaged, you're human, it hurts," he told BBC Radio Manchester. He said the site had been targeted before. "The objective is to balance access and community benefit with protecting and enhancing the natural environment, and that's one of the things that we're trying to make very clear to people." Image source, Believe Achieve CIC Image caption, Tunde Olasupo thanked residents who had shown the project support Believe Achieve CIC was set up in memory of Olasupo's son, Kingsley, who died in 2019, with the aim of giving young people opportunities he never got to experience. title: Man charged over Manchester synagogue attack

input.lead: Police say the man is accused of failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity
input.summary: Police say the man is accused of failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity
input.evidence_text: Man charged over Manchester synagogue attack - BBC News Image source, PA Media Image caption, The charges are linked to the 2 October 2025 attack By Paul Burnell North West Published 20 August 2026 A man has been charged in connection with the Manchester synagogue attack in which two men were killed. Counter terrorism police said Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, 49, of St James Road, Higher Broughton, Salford, had been charged with failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity. Hakim has been remanded into custody to appear before Westminster Magistrates' Court on Friday. There have so far been eight arrests in connection with the attack, however this is the first charge that "relates directly" to the morning of 2 October, when two men died as the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue was attacked by Jihad Al-Shamie. He was shot by police and died at the scene. Worshippers Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed. Assistant Chief Constable Rob Potts, from Counter Terrorism Policing North West (CTPNW) , said: "This is a significant development in our investigation, and my thoughts are with all those affected by the attack, particularly the bereaved loved ones and survivors. "We have updated them and continue to offer them as much support as possible. "Since the attack took place, we have been unwavering in our commitment to establishing the full picture behind the incident and identifying anybody who may have been involved in any way." In July, Mohammad Bashir, 31, who planned an attack on a military base with the Manchester synagogue attacker was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years. title: North West NHS trust accused of failing to investigate deaths

input.lead: Northern Care Alliance has responded to claims raised by an investigation
input.summary: Northern Care Alliance has responded to claims raised by an investigation
input.evidence_text: One of the north-west of England's biggest healthcare trusts has responded to allegations it failed to properly investigate claims patients died or were harmed during surgery Northern Care Alliance (NCA), which runs four hospitals in Greater Manchester, including Salford Royal Hospital, was put under an NHS enforcement notice to improve patient safety, in June But whistle blowers have now told an investigation by the Independent and Channel 4 , external that they were discouraged from reporting concerns The trust has told the BBC it is working to address staff concerns and has "clear processes to investigate incidents" A spokesperson for NCA said the trust changed the way it was organised in response to demands by NHS England to improve standards in surgical wards, tackling backlogs in spinal and gynaecology services But the investigation found patients are alleged to have been "left dying or in pain" in overcrowded A&E corridors, before then receiving invasive treatments which might have been avoided if there was no delay, the investigation claims

title: Six men held after Salford raids target heroin and cocaine supply

input.lead: Six men are arrested after early morning raids on homes in Salford
input.summary: Six men are arrested after early morning raids on homes in Salford
input.evidence_text: Six men held after Salford raids target heroin and cocaine supply - BBC News Image caption, Six men were arrested in early morning raids By Richard Stead Reporting from in Salford Published 20 August 2026 Six men have been arrested in drugs raids which aimed to target the supply of heroin and crack cocaine in Salford. About 50 police officers were involved in the operation, which took place at five addresses in the Pendlebury and Clifton areas of the city at 0530 BST. Officers seized drugs which are believed to be cocaine and heroin, cash and two high-value mountain bikes, which are suspected to have been stolen. Ch Insp Lee Gridley said the raids were the "result of months of evidence gathering" by Swinton's neighbourhood teams to "take action against people who prey on the vulnerable". He added: "Hopefully this operation will disrupt the supply of Class A drugs across Salford and all we can do is ask communities to give us the information we need and we will act robustly." Image caption, Chief Inspector Lee Gridley urges people to give information to police Police rammed the front doors off their hinges before entering the houses and flats to search the properties and make arrests. Four of the addresses were on Hopwood Street, Pendlebury and the fifth was a flat on Castleway in the Clifton area. Image caption, Part of the operation was on Hopwood Street in Pendlebury Those arrested in the raids are being questioned over a range of suspected offences. They include possession of Class A drugs, possession with intent to supply, possession of an offensive weapon, burglary and failure to appear at court. It was unveiled last week at a ceremony organised by Trafford Council’s Local Studies team, attended by residents, historians, council members, Connor Rand MP and the Friends of Bowd Wood, born in 1782, was a wool merchant who began campaigning in 1826 after seeing a young boy fall to his death inside a chimney onto a live fire. “Climbing boys” were children sent up chimneys to sweep them, often suffering burns, respiratory illness, deformity and suffocation From Bowdon he funded prosecutions against master sweeps who broke child labour laws, put up placards at railway stations and wrote to newspapers He also challenged magistrates and even Queen Victoria over the use of a child sweep at Windsor Castle His work with Lord Shaftesbury included testimony to the House of Lords in 1853, which helped lead to the Chimney Sweepers Act of 1875. Wood died in 1868, aged 85, seven years before the practice was banned. Six chimney sweeps from five towns carried his coffin to St Mary’s Churc

input.summary: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs)
input.evidence_text: Bolton Council is launching a new licensing scheme for landlords of houses in multiple occupation (HMOs) The scheme is designed to improve property conditions, strengthen management standards, and ensure tenants have access to safe, high-quality accommodation and was agreed at a meeting of Bolton Council’s Cabinet on Monday (August 17) HMOs are properties that are occupied by three or more people from different households, who share at least one basic amenity i.e. a kitchen, bathroom or toilet - the definition includes bedsits, shared houses and some self–contained flats that did not meet the required standard It is unacceptable that landlords cut corners in critical areas such as failing to obtain fire, gas, and electrical safety certificates or ensuring properties are safe Many landlords operate responsibly, but a substantial proportion of HMOs are poorly managed, unsafe and impact on the community In the past three years, the council has received 1,885 complaints about disrepair in rented homes, typically relating to fire safety, electrical and structural defects, overcrowding, cold and damp, and poor waste management and pest control
